The energetics of Escherichia coli during aerobic growth in continuous culture

Abstract
1. The energetics of Escherichia coli W growing aerobically in continuous culture have been investigated. Conditions were chosen such that growth was limited by the availability of carbon or oxygen (energy-limited cultures), or of ammonium of sulphate ions (excess energy cultures). 2. Under glycerol-limited conditions YmaxO2 (true molar growth yield with respect to oxygen) and YmaxATP (true molar growth yield with respect to ATP equivalents) were 50.9 g cells-mol O-02(-1) and 12.7 g cells-mol ATP equivalents-1 respectively; these values were not substantially altered during growth limited by oxygen, ammonium or sulphate. In contrast, M (the energy requirement for maintenance purposes) increased from approximately 2 mmol ATP equivalents-h-1-g cells-1 during energy-limited growth to 16.8 and 30.8 mmole ATP equivalents-h-1-g cells-1 when growth was limited by ammonium and sulphate ions respectively. 3. Replacement of glycerol by other limiting carbon sources caused YmaxATP to alter within the range 13.9 (glucose) to 7.1 (acetate) g cells-mol ATP equivalents-1 in the order glucose greater than galactose greather than arabinose greater than fructose greater than glycerol greater than fumarate greater than lactate greater than pyruvate greater than acetate. In each case the experimental value of YmaxATP was less than or equal to 55% of the theoretical value calculated from the known energy requirements for the biosynthesis of cell materials. 4. It is concluded from these results that neither M nor Ymax ATP are constant values for E. coli. M varies with the energy supply, being highest under excess energy growth conditions where it may reflect energy wastage by the cell. On the other hand, YmaxATP varies with the nature of the growth substrate and thus reflects the different energy requirements for the synthesis of cell material from different carbon sources.

Molar growth yields on oxygen or carbon substrate reflect the efficiency with which aerobic bacteria conserve energyvia substrate-level and oxidative phosphor yl ation, and subsequently utilise this energy for growth. Yields are most easily expressed in terms of the consumption of gaseous oxygen rather than of the carbon source since the former, unlike the latter, is rarely incorporated into cell material and is used solely as a terminal oxidant for respiration. In theory,  $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{m a x}$  is attained only at an infinite growth rate, since at lower growth rates a significant proportion of the total oxygen consumption is associated with the conservation of energy which is subsequently used for maintenance purposes rather than for growth [1]. In practice, it is possible to determine   $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  graphically by plotting the respiratory activity in situ of a con- tin u o us culture as a function of dilution rate  $[2\!-\!7]$  

The molar growth yield with respect toATP equivalents (YAx), reflects the efficiency with which cells utilise their conserved energy and can be calculated from  $Y_{0_{2}}^{\mathbf{max}}$   provided that the overall efficiency of aerobic energy  conservation  is accurately known. Measurement of the latter has proved difficult and the results have not been entirely consistent[8-10j However, the problem has been greatly simplified by the recent advent of techniques based on Mitchell's che mi osmotic hypothesis of oxidative phosphor yl a- tion[11],via which it is possible to measure the eff i- cie n cy of respiration-linked proton translocation in intact bacteria[12,13].Thus,batch cultures ofEscherich i a coli have been shown to exhibit  $\rightarrow\mathrm{H^{+}/O}$  ratios of approximately  $4{\mathrm{~\bfg}}$  -ion  $\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathbf{g}.$  -atom O for the oxidation of endogenous or  $\mathrm{NAD^{+}}$  -linked substrates  $[13-$  16l.a value which is commensurate with a  $\mathsf{P}/\mathrm{O}$  ratio of 2 assuming an  $\to{\mathrm{~H^{+}/P~}}$   ratio of  $2\ \mathbf{g}$  -ion  ${\mathrm{H}}^{+}/{\mathrm{mol}}$  phosphate ester if i ed[i1].The overall efficiency of aerobic energy conservation can thus be calculated from a knowledge of the efficiency of oxidative ph osph or vl ation and of the extent of substrate-level phosphor yl ation.  

In this paper we report the results of investigations into the energetics of  $E$  coli during aerobic growth in continuous culture under a variety of nutrient limit ations.Throughthe combined measurement of  $\to\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{O}$  ratios and  $Y_{0_{2}}^{\mathfrak{m a x}}$   we  have  attempted  to calculate unambiguous values for YAr p and  $M$  witha view to assessing both the extent to which these paramet ers are independent of culture conditions,andthe amountof energy which is utilised by the organism for purposes other than biosynthesis or maintenance.  

# MATERIALS AND METHODS  

# Culture Conditions  

E.coli W was grown at  $30~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$  in continuous culture using ache most at of the type described by Baker [17].The capacity of the che most at was  $500\,{\mathrm{-}}\,700~{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{l}}$  according to the aeration conditions employed, the latter being determined by a captive bar magnet under the control of a magnetic stirrer. The culture medium const it ed of a minimal salts solution[18]supplemented with n it r ilo-tri acetic acid  $(0.1\ \mathrm{g/l})$  and the chosen carbon source  $(30~\mathrm{mM})$  .The following modifications were made for the different growth conditions employed:carbon-limited(  $7.0\:\mathrm{mM}$  carbon source,except for sugars which were  $5\:\mathrm{mM}$  ammonium-limited  $\mathrm{1.5\,mM\,NH_{4}C l}$  ,sulphate-limited  $(14.6~\upmu\mathrm{M}~\mathrm{K}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4})$  .These concentrations were selected following determinations of cell yield as a function of limiting nutrient concentration in small-scale batch cultures. For oxygen-limited growth the complete medium was used but the stirring rate was decreased until the concentration of dissolved oxygen in the culture was essentially zero.  

# Respiratory Activity in situ  

The respiratory activities in situ (mol  $\mathrm{O}_{2}\cdot\mathtt{h}^{-1}\cdot\mathtt{g}$   $\mathbf{cells}^{-1}$  ) of growing cells were determined by measuring the difference in the concentration of oxygen between input and effluent air of chemostat cultures using a Clark oxygen electrode mounted in the air stream. Concomitant as say of the air flow rate(corrected for the influence of the medium flow rate and for water vapour pressure),together with the volume and density of the culture,allowed calculation of the specific respiratory activity which was subsequently corrected for deviation from standard temperature. Full details of this technique, which was developed from a method described by Hayes et al. [19], have been reported in previous communications from this laboratory [5,6].  

Values for  $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  and  $M_{0_{2}}$  were determined from the slope and intercept respectively of linear plots of  $Q\mathrm{o}_{2}$  in situ versus dilution rate.Each plot was comprised of an average of 8 points to which the best line was fitted by linear regression analysis using a HewlettPackard 1600B bench top computer. The average percentage standard errors in  $Y_{0_{2}}^{\mathtt{m a x}}$  and  $M_{0_{2}}$  for the twelve determinations reported in this paper were  $8.7\,\%$  and  $30.0\,\%$  respectively.  

# Cell Composition and Activity  

Whole cell protein content was determined colou ri metrically using Fol in's reagent[20].Glycogen was extracted quantitatively from whole cells[21] and subsequently assayed colour i metrically using anthrone reagent[22]. Glycerol kinase and glycerol dehydrogenase activities of cell free extracts were assayed by standard procedures [23,24].

# Preparation and Assay of Respiratory Membranes  

Respiratory membranes were prepared and assayed for cytochrome content as described previously [16 26,27].  

# Effluent Growth Medium Composition  

The concentration of acetate in effluent growth media was determined either by gas-liquid chromatographyat  $210~^{\circ}\mathbf{C}$  using a Pye 104 chromatograph (flame ionisation detector) fitted with a Poropak Q column (courtesy of Dr J. W. Drozd, Shell Research Ltd., Sitting bourne, England) or by standard colourimetric procedures [28]. Lactate, pyruvate and 2-oxo- glut a rate were assayed by standard enzymatic tech- niques [23].  

# RESULTS  

Glycerol-limited cultures of  $E$  coli exhibited respira tory activities in situ which increased linearly as a function of dilution rate (Fig.1). These cultures thus appeared tobehave according tothe equation proposed by Harrison and Loveless [2] for aerobic, energy-limited growth,viz.  

$$
Q_{0_{2}}=\frac{\mu}{Y_{\mathrm{ATP}}^{\operatorname*{max}}\cdot N}+\frac{M}{N}\,.
$$  

Since the slope is equivalent to  $1/Y_{\mathrm{ATP}}^{\operatorname*{max}}\cdot N$   $(\,\equiv\,1/Y_{{\mathrm O}_{2}}^{\tt m a x})$   and the intercept is equivalent to  $M/N$   $(\equiv\,M_{\mathrm{O}_{2}})$  ,these cultures of  $E$  coli exhibited a  $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  of

  $50.9\mathrm{~g~}$  cells  $\cdot$  mol  $\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-1}$  andan  $M_{0_{2}}$  of  $0.58\;\mathrm{mmoI}$   $\mathrm{O}_{2}\cdot\dot{\mathsf{h}}^{-1}\cdot\mathsf{g}\,\mathsf{c e l l s}^{-1}$  (Table 1).  

The culture density increased slightly with dilution rate, as might be expected where the limiting nutrient was the source both of carbon and energy, but both theprotein contentof the cells and the  ${\rightarrow\mathrm{H^{+}/O}}$  ratio for the oxidation of endogenous substrates were essentially constant over the wide range of dilution rates employed.Only acetate was detected in the efluent growth medium.The concentration of the latter was very low, thus indicating that partial oxidation of the carbon source (with a concomitant increase in the yield of ATP from substrate-level cf. oxidative phosp hory la tion, and hence an over estimation of  $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  did not occur to any significant extent.Since  $E$  coli exhibits proton-trans locating segments 1 and 2 only

 [13,16,29],the endogenous  ${\rightarrow{\mathrm{H}}^{+}/\mathrm{O}}$  ratio of 3.96

  $\pm\:0.07$  g-ion  $\mathrm{H^{+}}$  ·g-atom  $\mathrm{O}^{-1}$  which was observed with these glycerol-limited cultures suggested that the major endogenous substrate was reduced pyr i dine nucleotide.  

In contrast to glycerol-limitation, the growth of  $E$  . coli under oxygen-limited conditions was characterised by a sharp break in the plot of  $Q\mathrm{o}_{2}$  in situ versus dilution rate (Fig.2). At dilution rates  $\leq0.14\mathrm{~h~}^{\sim1}$  the plot was clearly linear and yielded a  $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  of  $50.2\;\mathrm{g}$  cells  $\cdot$  mol  $\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-1}$   and a maintenance respiration rate of  $0.54\;\mathrm{mm}\,{\mathrm{O}}_{2}\cdot\mathrm{h}^{-1}\cdot\mathrm{g}\,\mathrm{cells}^{-1}$  (Table 1), values which were very close to those obtained with glycerol

This break in the graph was clearly not caused by a sudden change in either the cell composition (the protein content was unaltered over the entire range of dilution rates employed), the stoic hio me try of respiration-linked proton translocation or the concentration of glycerol oxidation products in the effluent growth medium (only acetate was detected and its concentration was again very low). The reason for the sharp increase in the apparent value of  $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  at  $D>0.14\,\mathrm{h}^{-1}$  is therefore unclear.  

The rather low endogenous  $\rightarrow\mathrm{H^{+}/O}$  ratios which were observed with oxygen-limited cultures(3.36  $\pm\ 0.05\:\mathrm{g}$  -ion  $\mathrm{H}^{+}\cdot\mathbf{g}$  -atom  $\mathrm{O^{-1}}$  )indicated the use of between one and two proton-trans locating segments for the oxidation of endogenous substrates compared with the full two segments in glycerol-limited cultures. The most likely explanation of this observation is that the endogenous substrate pool has shifted to a higher redox level under these growth conditions (i.e. it is now composedof amixture of  $\mathrm{N}\mathrm{A}\mathrm{D}^{\pm}$  linked and flavin-linked substrates). This conclusion is supported by the observation that such cells exhibit  $\rightarrow\mathrm{H^{+}/O}$  ratios commensurate with the presence of two protontrans locating segments when starved and subsequently loadedwith  $\tt N A D^{+}$  -linked substrates.In contrast to the other nutrient limitations employed in this study, the culture density of oxygen-limited cultures decreased considerably as a function of increasing dilution rate,a phenomenon which can readily be explained in terms of the balance between the supply and utilisation of oxygen. The low stirring rate provides a poor but constant supply of oxygen to the culture; this is matched by the total respiratory activity of the culture [measuredas  $0.458\,\pm\,0.019$  (11) mmol  $\mathrm{O}_{2}\cdot\mathsf{h}^{-1}\cdot1^{-1}]$  with the result that the dissolved oxygen concentration is extremely low. Since the specific respiratory activityin situ increases with dilution rate,the cell density must decrease.  

Ammonium-limited culturesof  $E$  coli also exhibited linear plots of  $Q\mathrm{o}_{2}$  in situ versus dilution rate to yield  $Y_{0_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  of  $57.2\;\mathrm{g\,cells\cdotmol\,O_{2}^{-1}}$  and a considerably increased maintenance respiration rate of  $4.20~\mathrm{mm}$   $\mathrm{O}_{2}\cdot\mathrm{h}^{-1}\cdot\mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{cells}^{-1}$  (Fig.3; Table 1). The cell density decreased slightly with increasing dilution rate but the endogenous   ${\rightarrow\mathrm{H^{+}/O}}$  ratios were essentially constant and indicated the presence of two protontrans locating segments with NADH as the major endogenous substrate. In contrast to either glycerollimited or oxygen-limited cultures, the cellular protein content increased significantly with increasing dilution rate, but this was matched by a corresponding decrease in the glycogen content of the cells.  

With sulphate-limited cultures of  $E$  .coli the relationship between  $Q_{0_{2}}$   in situ and dilution rate was also linear and reflected a  $Y_{0_{2}}^{\mathtt{m a x}}$  of  $54.6~\mathrm{g}$  cells  $^*$  mol  $\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-1}$   together with an extremely high maintenance respiration rate  of   $7\cdot70\;\mathrm{mmol}$   $\mathrm{O}_{2}\cdot\mathtt{h}^{-1}\cdot\mathtt{g}$   cells -1 (Table 1). The  ${\rightarrow\mathrm{H^{+}/O}}$  ratios for the oxidation of endogenous substrates were virtually identical to those observed for glycerol-limited or ammoniumlimited cultures and were essentially constant as a function of dilution rate, as also was the cellular protein content. The effluent growth media from both  the  ammonium-limited  and  sulphate-limited cultures contained only very low concentrations of acetate, thus indicating that even under non-energylimited conditions partial oxidation of glycerol was only very slight; no other partial oxidation products of glycerol were detected.  

Room temperature difference spectra of respiratory membranes prepared from cultures limited by glycerol, ammonium or sulphate indicated the presence of cytochrome  $b_{556}$  and cytochrome oxidase  $^o$  .Membranes prepared from oxygen-limited cultures contained, in addition, cytochrome oxidases   $a_{1}$  and  $d(a_{2})$  ; the appearance of these latter two cytochrome s is a characteristic and well documented response of this strain of  $E$  coli to the lowered availability of the terminal electron acceptor [26].  

In order to calculate  $Y_{\mathrm{ATP}}^{\operatorname*{max}}$  and  $M$  from the values of  $Y_{0_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  and  $M_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}$   determined above, it is necessary to know the value of  $N$  .The complete oxidation of one mole of glycerol by  $E$  .coli yields five moles of reduced pyridine nucleotide (via gly cer aldehyde-3- phosphate dehydrogenase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, 2-oxo glutarate dehydrogen asean dma late dehydrogenase)and two moles of reduced favin (via glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and succinate dehydrogenase)(see [13]; also I. S. Farmer, and C. W. Jones, unpublished data). In addition, three moles of ATP (or an energetically equivalent nucleotide)are produced by substratelevel phosphor yl ation (via ph os p hog lyc e rate kinase, pyruvate kinase and succinic thiokinase)although one of these is consumed by glycerol kinase. Since the respiratory system of  $E$  .coli contains proton-translocating segments 1 and 2 [13,15,16] then, assuming  $\tt a n\rightarrow H^{+}/A T P$  ratio of 2 [11], the complete oxidation of one mole of glycerol(  $\it\Omega\equiv3.5\;\mathrm{mol}$  of oxygen reduced) yields 14 moles of ATP.  $N$  is therefore equalto  $4.00\,\mathrm{mol}$  ATP equivalents  $^{\ast}$  mol  $\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-1}$  . Analysis of the enzymes which cat aly se the catabolism of glycerol in  $E$  coli indicated that, in contrast to Klebsiella aerogenes [30], the glycerol kinase/glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenaseroute was predominant under both glycerollimited and excess glycerol growth conditions; no  $\mathrm{NAD^{+}}$  -linked glycerol dehydrogenase activity could be detected in cell-free extracts of either type of culture. Thus, there is no evidence to suggest that the value of  $N$  alters with the nature of the limiting nutrient provided that glycerol remains the sole carbon source. When the energetics of  $E$  coli cultures growing on different carbon sources were compared, the   $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  values were found to vary from 20.3 to  $59.7~\mathrm{g}$  cells  $\cdot\bmod{\mathrm{O}}_{2}^{-1}$  consumed (Table 2). The endogenous  ${\rightarrow}\,\mathrm{H}^{+}/$  O ratios of these cultures continued to reflect the presence of two proton-trans locating segments in the respiratory chain,although they also pointed to slight alterations in the content of the endogenous substrate pool. The  $N$  values which were subsequently calculated for the oxidation of the different carbon substrates showed only a relatively small variation (2.88 to 4.33), thus indicating that the observed changes in the values of  $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  principally refeted variation in the values of  $\bar{Y_{\mathrm{ATP}}^{\mathfrak{m a x}}}$  , viz. from  $7.1\ \mathrm{g}$  cells  $\cdot$  mol ATP equivalents  $^{-1}$  for growth on acetate to  $13.9\ \mathrm{g}$  cells  $\cdot$  mol ATP equivalents  $^{-1}$  when glucose was the carbon source. Analysis of the effuent growth media indicated that oxidation of each of the different carbon sources was essentially complete (even during growth on glucose less than  $0.40~\mathrm{mM}$  acetatewas detected). The experimentally determined values of YATp were between 38 and  $55\,\%$   of the theoretical values for all of the carbon sources tested (the theoretical Yxrp was calculated from the known energy requirements for the biosynthesis of cell materials as described by Stouthamer [31]). These figures indicated that at least  $45\,\%$   of the total energy which is consumed for growth-rate-dependent processes cannot be accounted for by simple bio synthetic considerations and must therefore reflect other energy-dependent cellular events.  

Thevalueof  $M$  also varied with growth on the different carbon sources, but no consistent pattern was observed.The value was always relatively small  $\c=4.5$  mmol ATP equivalents  $\cdot\:\mathsf{h}^{-1}\cdot\mathsf{g}\;\mathsf{c e l l s}^{-1})$  and was thus commensurate with the carbon (and energy)- limited status of these cultures.

The failure of sulphate-limited cultures to exhibit lowered  ${\rightarrow}\mathrm{H^{+}/O}$  ratios is in direct contrast torecent reports by Poole and Haddock [37,38] which claimed  $\to\mathrm{H^{+}/O}$   ratios of approximately two for the oxidation of endogenous,  $\mathrm{NAD^{+}}$  -linked andflavin-linked substrates by sulphate-limited cultures of E. coli K12 (strain C-1 S).  

It is clear from our studies with  $E$  coli W growing on glycerol that   $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$   is essentially independent of the nature of the growth-limiting nutrient, although at any given dilution rate the  $Q\mathrm{o}_{2}$  in situ is substantially higher in cultures which have an ample supply of energy (i.e. where the limiting nutrient is ammonium or sulphate ions). The latter phenomenon reflects the very high maintenance respiration rates ofthese cultures compared with energy-limited cultures. It is likely therefore that theverylow  $Y_{0}$  values which have recently been reported for sulphate-limited culturesof  $E$  .coli[37,38]and Klebsiella(Aerobacter) aero genes 30],r effect the fact that  $Y_{0}$  was determined only at a single dilution rate and that no correction was made for the veryhigh maintenance respiration rates.  

Following avery careful study of the energetics of  $K_{\ell}$  aero genes growing in continuous culture with glucose as carbon source,Stouthamer andBetten- haussen [3] concluded that the respiratory chain energy conservation efficiency of this organism was severely diminished under sulphate-limited conditions and that most of the energy was conserved via substrate level phosphor yl ation. They reported a linear relationship between  $Q\mathrm{o}_{2}$  in situ and dilution rate, with a slope equivalent to a  $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$   of approximately  $47~\mathrm{g}$  cells  $\cdot$  mol  $\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-1}$  (very similar to thevalue for glucose-limited growth) and an intercept equiva lent to the very high maintenance respiration rate of  $4.9\;\mathrm{mmol}$   $\dot{\mathrm{O}_{2}}\cdot\dot{\mathrm{h}^{-1}}\cdot\mathrm{g}\,\mathrm{cells}^{-1}$  .Very importantly, however,they also detected substantial levels of acetatein the spent growth medium which indicated that the glucose was undergoing only partial oxidation (see also [39]). Furthermore, in spite of being present in relatively high concentrations in the inflowing growth medium,the glucose was always completely consumed by the culture. After correcting for these observations,a  $\mathrm{P/O}$  ratioof substantially less than1 was calculated for the oxidation of endogenous substrates. In contrast, our studies with sulphatelimited cultures of  $E.$  coli growing on glycerol have revealed that partial oxidation of thelatter is only ver vs light and that substantial concentrations of glycerol are still present in the effluent growth medium. Similar results have also been reported for sulphate  

limited cultures of  $K$  .aero genes utilising glycerol as their sole source of carbon[39].It would appear therefore that the growth of  $K$  .aerogenes and  $E.$  coli under sulphate-limited conditions is not accompanied by a significant change in the value of  $Y_{0_{2}}^{\mathsf{m a x}}$  , although the reason for this appears to vary with the nature of the carbon source. In the presence of glucose, partial oxidation leads to increased energy conservation via substrate level phosphor yl ation,but the effect of this on  $Y_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}^{\mathrm{max}}$  is offset by a low  $\mathrm{P/O}$  ratio [3]. In contrast, partial oxidation of glycerol is only slight and energy conservation is effected principally via a well coupled respiratory system.  

There is, however, general agreement that sulphatelimitation(like theearlier documented cases of nitrogen-limitation[6,4o]) causes a substantial increase in the maintenance coefficient, presumably via some form of energy wastage. The mechanism of this process, which occurs only under excess energy growth conditions and is independent of the nature of the carbon source,is unclear.It undoubtedly reflects the partial uncoupling of energy-conserving and energy-utilising cellular reactions, possibly via enhanced ATPase activity[3],and merits further experimental attention.  

The  $Y_{\mathbf{ATP}}^{\operatorname*{max}}$  of  $12.7~\mathrm{g}$  cells  $\cdot$  mol ATP equivalents-1 whichwas determined for the glycerol-limited growth of  $E.$  .coli W agrees well with the value of 13.5whichwas calculated for the growth of Bacillus mega teri umD 440 under the same conditions [5,6]. However, it is clear from our results that the experimental value of Yxtp varies dramatically with the nature of the carbon sourcein the order glucose  $>$  galactose  $>$  arabinose  $>$  fructose  $>$  glycerol  $>$  fumarate  $>$  lactate  $>$  pyr- uvate  $>$   acetate. The differences appear to reflect the different energy requirements for the conversion of the various carbon substrates into cell material and have been predicted elsewhere from theoretical conside rations [31,41,42]. The concept that YAtp is a constant value of  $10.6~\mathrm{g}$  cells/mol ATP equivalents [43] is therefore no longer acceptable. These results are in broad agreement with earlier reports that lower  $Y_{0}$  valueswere observed during the batch growth of  $K.$  aerogenes on tri carboxylic acid intermediates compared with sugars 44,45],and of they east Candida util is on acetate or ethanol compared with glucose[46] On the other hand,theyare clearly at variance with the recent report by Hempfling and Mainzer [7] that the growth efficiencies of continuous cultures of  $E$  coli Bon different carbon sources were in the order glycerol  $>$  acetate  $>$  galactose  $>$  glucose.  

The large discrepancy between the experimental and theoretical values of Ymrpwhich we observed with  $E$  coli W during carbon-limited growth presumably reflects the use of energy for growth-rate-dependent processes other than simple biosynthesis.Ofthese, the active transport of the carbon substrate maybe a significant component,particularly when thelatter is a relatively small and/or highly oxidised molecule (such that a relatively large number of molecules must be transported in order to effect a unit amount of energy conservation and cell biosynthesis). The entryof inorganic nutrients[47,48],the ejection of unwanted materials (particularly  $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$  [49]andthe extra biosynthesis engendered by macromolecular turnover [5o]may also contribute significantly to total energy consumption.

Changes in the proton potential and the cellular energetics of Escherichia coli during growth by aerobic and anaerobic respiration or by fermentation

Abstract
The energetic parameters of Escherichia coli were analyzed for the aerobic/anaerobic transition. The electrochemical proton potential (Δ p) across the cytoplasmic membrane was determined in the steady state of respiration with O2, nitrate, fumarate, dimethylsulfoxide (Me2SO), and for fermentation. With O2, a proton potential of −160 mV was obtained. For anaerobic respiration with nitrate, fumarate or Me2SO, Δ p decreased only slightly by about 20 mV in contrast to earlier assumptions, whereas Δ p dropped by approximately 40 mV during fermentation. Under all conditions, the membrane potential (Δ @KY) contributed the major portion to Δ p. The cellular ATP levels were highest for aerobic growth (about 13 μmol/g dry cells) and decreased to 3−6 μmol/g in anaerobic metabolism. Δ .cf2.G.cf2..cf1..es.cf1.′.cf5..rb.eiPhos.rb, however, was constant due to equivalent changes of the ADP contents. Transition to the stationary growth phase caused a massive drop in the ATP content. It is concluded that, during anaerobic respiration, the energetic situation for the bacteria is very similar to that for aerobic growth with respect to Δ .cf2.G.cf2..cf1..es.cf1.′.cf5..rb.eiPhos.rb and Δ p whereas, for fermentation, a significant decrease in Δ p was observed. The consequences for the cellular energetics and for the regulation of the aerobic/anaerobic transition are discussed.

Keywords:  proton potential; membrane potential; anaerobic respiration, aerobic/anaerobic transition; Escherichia coli . Facultative anaerobes such as  Escherichia coli  are capable of growth both under oxic and anoxic conditions. The energetics and the ATP yields vary considerably for both conditions (Unden and Bongaerts,  1 997). The free energy for glucose oxidation with   $\mathrm{O}_{2}$     $(\mathcal{A}\,G_{0}^{\prime}=-2870~\mathrm{kJ/mol}$   glucose) exceeds that for glucose fermentation   $(\varDelta G_{0}^{\prime}=-218\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}$   glucose). Similarly, respiration with NADH yields much higher free energy with   $\mathrm{O}_{2}$   $(\varDelta G_{0}^{\prime}=-233\;\mathrm{kJ/mol}$   NADH) than with fumarate (  $\mathcal{A}G_{0}^{\prime}=$   $-67\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$   NADH). Therefore, it has been claimed that the proton potential   $(\varDelta p)$   and the phosphor yl ation potential   $(\varDelta G_{\mathrm{Phos}}^{\prime})$   of  $E.$  . coli  are decreased significantly under anoxic conditions. Although the respective energetic parameters have been analyzed repeatedly (Cole et al.,  1 967; Hell ing we rf et al.,  1 98 1 ; Kashket et al.,  1 98 1 ,  1 982,  1 983) this question has not been solved. In particular, the data are not complete and consider only the situation for aerobic respiration and fermentation, but not for anaerobic respiration. In addition the parameters of the various studies were not performed in a systematic manner which allowed direct comparison.  

This obvious lack in our knowledge on the energetic parameters of facultative anaerobic metabolism is contrasted by the significance of such parameters for the aerobic/anaerobic transition. There are indications that the proton potential has to be lowered in anaerobic respiration to enable the functioning of coupling enzymes such as NADH dehydrogenase I ( nuo  genes) as a proton pump (Bongaerts et al.,  1 995; Tran et al.,  1 997; Unden and Bongaerts,  1 997). In fumarate or dimethyl sulfoxide   $(\mathbf{MeV}_{2}\mathbf{SO})$  respiration, the enzyme has to use men aquino ne or demethylmen aquino ne as an electron acceptor (Tran et al.,  1 997). The electro-negative midpoint potential of men aquino ne   $\begin{array}{r l}{\relax(E^{\circ\prime}=}\end{array}$   $-80\:\mathrm{mV})$   results in a low redox difference between NADH

  $(E^{\circ\prime}=-320~\mathrm{mV})$  ) and men aquino ne. Under these conditions, NADH dehydrogenase I would be able to operate as a proton pump with the suggested ratio of   $2\mathrm{~\H^{+}/e^{-}}$    only at decreased membrane potentials. Moreover, it has been suggested that the presumed drop in  $\varDelta p$   between aerobic and anaerobic respiratory conditions could supply the regulatory signal for the   $\mathrm{O}_{2}$   sensor protein ArcB (Bogachev et al.,  1 993,  1 995) which is one of the major transcriptional regulators of aerobic and anaerobic metabolism (Iuchi and Lin,  1 993). In light of these deficites in our knowledge on the energetic status of    $E_{\uparrow}$  . coli  during aerobic and anaerobic growth, the membrane   $(\varDelta\varPsi)$  , proton   $(\varDelta p)$   and phosp hory la tion   $(\varDelta G_{\mathrm{Phos}}^{\prime})$   potentials were determined under conditions of aerobic and anaerobic respiration and of fermentation, in a manner which enabled direct comparison. It was shown that, in contrast to earlier assumptions, there are only minor changes in  $\varDelta\varPsi$  ,  $\varDelta p$   and  $\it{A G_{\mathrm{Phos}}^{\prime}}$   after switching from aerobic to anaerobic respiration. A more significant decrease in  $\varDelta\varPsi$   and  $\varDelta p$   was only observed for fermentation.

# DISCUSSION  

ATP contents and  $\mathbf{\it{4G}_{\mathbf{oplus}}^{\prime}}$   as energetic parameters for faculta- tive anaerobic metabolism.  The ATP contents and  $\it{4G_{\mathrm{phys}}^{\prime}}$   were compared for    $E$  . coli  growing with various electron acceptors under oxic and anoxic conditions. The electron acceptors were the only varied parameters, to enable direct comparison. The values were at the upper level of previously published values (Mathis and Brown,  1 976; Holms et al.,  1 972; Cole et al.,  1 967; Lowry et al.,  1 97 1 ). The ATP contents not only decreased for fermentation (factor 2.4), but also for anaerobic respiration, in particular for  $\mathrm{Ma}_{2}\mathrm{SO}$   (factor 4.5) and fumarate (factor 2.6) respirations. The contents are not related to the aerobic/anaerobic transition, but there is a loose relation to the growth rates (Table 4) which had already been observed earlier (Bagnara and Finch, 1 973). The  $\varDelta G_{\mathrm{Phos}}^{\prime}$   values, however, were remarkably constant for the various conditions due to the corresponding changes in the ADP contents. Therefore,    $\it{\Delta}M G_{\mathrm{Phos}}^{\prime}$   cannot be used as a characteristic signal for the aerobic/anaerobic transition.  

High membrane   $(M\,\Psi)$   and proton   $(\pmb{M}p)$   potentials in anaerobic respiration.  The procedure of Zaritzky et al. ( 1 98 1 ) has been shown as a reliable procedure for measuring  $\varDelta\varPsi$   (Wloczyk et al.,  1 989; Mell et al.,  1 986). Here, for aerobic respiration,  $\varDelta\varPsi$   $(-140\:\mathrm{mV})$   and    $\varDelta p$   (  $.-160\;\mathrm{mV})$   values similar to earlier published data (Kashket et al.,  1 98 1 ;  1 982) were obtained. Most remarkably, the    $\varDelta p$   values (about    $-140\:\mathrm{mV})$  ) for anaerobic respiration with nitrate, fumarate and  $\mathrm{Mo}_{2}\mathrm{SO}$   decreased only up to  $20\:\mathrm{mV}$   compared to aerobic respiration. The results are in contrast to earlier experiments suggesting a decrease of    $\varDelta p$   for fumarate respiration to about    $-100\:\mathrm{mV}$   (Hell ing we rf et al.,  1 98 1 ). The presence of high    $\varDelta\varPsi$   and  $\varDelta p$   values in anaerobic respiration was also shown directly by measuring similar values when the same preparation of bacteria was incubated alternatively with  $\mathrm{O}_{2}$  or fumarate (Table 3). Thus, the situation for    $E$  . coli  appears to be similar to that for  Wolinella succ in o genes  which is known to build up high    $\varDelta p$   values   $(-170\:\mathrm{mV})$   with electro positive and electronegative acceptors (Wloczyk et al.,  1 989; Mell et al., 1 986). High  $\varDelta p$   values during aerobic and anaerobic respiration are essential for the function of ATP synthase. From the  $\varDelta p$   and the  $\varDelta G_{\mathrm{Phos}}^{\prime}$   values, it can be calculated that  $3.1\!-\!3.4~\!\mathrm{H}^{+}$    are required for ADP phosphor yl ation if    $\varDelta p$   and    $\it{\Delta}M G_{\mathrm{Phos}}^{\prime}$   are in thermodynamic equilibrium (Table 4). This is in agreement with suggested  $\mathrm{H^{+}/A T P}$   ratios of  $_{3-4}$  . A supposed decrease of    $\varDelta p$   to  $-100\:\mathrm{mV}$   would require  $\mathrm{H^{+}/A T P}$   ratios close to 5, which is very unlikely. Therefore, the    $\varDelta p$   of anaerobic respiration indeed has to be as high as determined here. Only in fermentation, when ADP is phosphor y late d by substrate-level phosphor yl ation, is a decrease in    $\varDelta p$   to lower levels tolerated.  

Significance of high    $_{4p}$   values for the function of anaerobic respiration.  In    $E$  . coli , fumarate and   $\mathrm{Mo}_{2}\mathrm{SO}$   respiration with NADH depends on the proton pumping NADH dehydrogenase I (Bongaerts et al.,  1 995; Tran et al.,  1 997) which is supposed to trans locate   $2~\mathrm{H^{+}/e^{-}}$    (Friedrich et al.,  1 995; Bogachev et al., 1 996). For operation in fumarate and  $\mathrm{Me}_{2}\mathrm{SO}$   respiration, NADH dehydrogenase I has to use the nap h tho quin ones (men aquino ne and de meth lyme na quin one) as the redox mediators (Wissenbach et al.,  1 990;  1 992; Tran et al.,  1 997). The redox reaction NADH  $\longrightarrow$  quinone has to provide the energy for the translocation of the protons over the membrane. With the electro-negative menaquinone, the translocation of maximally    $1.7\;\mathrm{H^{+}/e^{-}}$    can be driven at the    $\varDelta p$   values reported here (Table 5). Therefore, it was argued that high  $\varDelta p$   values would not be compatible with the functioning of NADH dehydrogenase I in fumarate or  $\mathrm{Me}_{2}\mathrm{SO}$   respiration as a  $\mathrm{H^{+}}$    pump (Bongaerts et al.,  1 995). However, with the more electro positive (minor) de methyl men aquino ne which is also present under these conditions, maximal  $\mathrm{H^{+}/e^{-}}$    ratios of 2.5 can be calculated, enabling the function of NADH dehydrogenase I as a proton pump. Additionally, the   $\mathrm{NADH/NAD^{+}}$    ratios are supposed to be increased under anoxic growth conditions. By this, the actual redox potential of the NADH/NAD 1   couple and the redox difference between donor (NADH) and the acceptor (nap h tho quin one) would further increase, facilitating proton translocation. Thus, functioning of NADH dehydrogenase I as a proton pump is possible at the    $\varDelta p$   values determined here, but not at values of    $-100~\mathrm{mV}$   determined earlier.  

Significance of    $\mathbfcal{A}\,\pmb{\Psi}$   values of aerobic and anaerobic respiration for the regulation of facultative metabolism.  Changes in  $\varDelta\varPsi$   and/or  $\varDelta p$   have been suggested to provide the signal for the aerobic/anaerobic transition to membrane o us  $\mathrm{O}_{2}$  -sensors such as ArcB of  $E$  . coli  (Bogachev et al.,  1 993,  1 995). The small differences for    $\varDelta\varPsi$   and    $\varDelta p$   for aerobic and anaerobic respiration described here argue against such a signalling function. The same applies to    $\varDelta\mathfrak{p}\mathrm{H}$   which is negligible and does not change significantly; only for the switch to fermentation do larger differences exist. It is, therefore, doubtful whether    $\varDelta\,\mathrm{pH}$   or    $\varDelta\varPsi$   can signal the state of   $\mathrm{O}_{2}$   supply to  $\mathrm{O}_{2}$  -sensors such as ArcB.
